sentences.text: Indosinosuchus was an extinct teleosaurid crocodilomorph, a group of ancient crocodile relatives.
The type species of the genus is Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis.
Its jaws held forty-seven teeth in the upper front, thirty in the upper side, and thirty-one in the lower jaw.
Every tooth was slender and conical with a curved crown, suited for gripping prey.
The snout tip formed by the premaxillae expanded moderately to the side, a trait that varies among teleosaurs.
Raised rims around the circular eye sockets gave the animal a telescopic appearance similar to modern gharials.
Unlike gharials, however, the eyes of Indosinosuchus were directed slightly towards the sides as well as upwards.
Armor plates called osteoderms covered its body, being wider than long on the trunk and longer than wide on the tail.
These osteoderms featured a front-to-back keel on top, while the underside was flat and lacked a keel.
Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis is the only named teleosaurid genus known from a freshwater environment, whereas most other members of the group are marine.
This species possessed the highest posterior mechanical advantage of any known teleosaur, indicating the greatest maximum force along its tooth row.
It also had the highest jaw-opening speed among teleosaurs, suggesting a very rapid bite mechanism.
The genus Indosinosuchus was initially described by Martin and colleagues in 2019.
By 2019, ten individuals ranging from juveniles to fully mature adults were known from the Phu Noi locality.
Specimen PRC-11, a complete skull and mandible, was designated the holotype for Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis.
In 2020, Johnson, Young, and Brusatte examined specimen PRC-239, which was previously referred to Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis.
A 2026 study by Lauprasert and colleagues questioned the validity of Indosinosuchus kalasinensis after examining material from Ban Nam Pun.
I. potamosiamensis had the highest jaw-opening speed among teleosaurs, whereas I. kalasinensis had a lower opening mechanical advantage, suggesting a faster bite.
One nearly complete specimen with an articulated vertebral column may have been preserved after the animal floated on water, lost its head, and was rapidly buried.
Marks from dermestid beetles on fossils suggest the carcasses dried out for at least 8 weeks, indicating preservation during a dry season.
Indosinosuchus is classified in the family Teleosauridae, though its robust skull resembles members of Machimosauridae.
Phylogenetic analysis suggests I. kalasinensis is the most basal member of Teleosauridae, while I. potamosinensis is more derived.
Two species, I. potamosiamensis and I. kalasinensis, are known from the Phu Kradung Formation.
The animal has a humerus to femur ratio of 0.63, consistent with its relatives.
Indosinosuchus is an extinct teleosaurid crocodilomorph that lived in Thailand during the Jurassic.
It lived in what is now Thailand during the Late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous.
The Phu Noi locality where I. potamosiamensis fossils were found represents an oxbow lake or abandoned river channel.
There is a debate regarding the age of the Phu Kradung Formation, with faunal evidence suggesting the Late Jurassic while zircon and palynological data suggest the Early Cretaceous.
A hypothesis suggests the formation straddles the Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary, marking the replacement of freshwater teleosaurs by goniopholids and pholidosaurids in the Cretaceous.
Researchers suggest the lack of recovered relationships between Indosinosuchus species in some studies may be due to insufficient fossil material and poor preservation of the postcranial skeleton.
It is debated whether the differences in bite mechanics between I. potamosiamensis and I. kalasinensis represent distinct ecological niches or are merely artifacts of post-mortem skull distortion.
It is debated whether the animals died in a flash flood or during a drought, with decomposition occurring as waters receded.
